resources.content:
## 1. Web Resources

A Web Resource is any data that can be obtained via internet.

A resource can be

- HTML document
- CSS document
- JSON Data or Plain text
- Image, Video, etc.

## 2. Uniform Resource Locator (URL)

URL is a text string that specifies where a resource can be found on the internet.

We can access web resources using the URL.

**Syntax:** `protocol://domainName/path?query-parameters`

In the URL `http://www.flipkart.com/watches?type=digital&rating=4`,

- `http` is a **Protocol**
- `www.flipkart.com` is a **Domain Name**
- `/watches` is a **Path**
- `type=digital&rating=4` is the **Query Parameters**

### 2.1 Protocol

A protocol is a standard set of rules that allow electronic devices to communicate with each other.

There are different types of protocols.

- Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP)
- Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS)
- Web Sockets, etc.

#### 2.1.1 HTTP

The Hypertext Transfer Protocol (HTTP), is a protocol used to transfer resources over the web.

Examples: Internet forums, Educational sites, etc.

**HTTP Request:** Message sent by the client

**HTTP Response:** Message sent by the server

#### 2.1.2 HTTPS

In Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure (HTTPS), information is transferred in an
encrypted format and provides secure communication.

Examples: Banking Websites, Payment gateway, Login Pages, Emails and Corporate Sector Websites, etc.

### 2.2 Domain Name

It indicates which Web server is being requested.

### 2.3 Path

The path is to identify the resources on the server.

Examples:

- **/watches** in `http://www.flipkart.com/watches`
- **/electronics/laptops/gaming** in `http://www.flipkart.com/electronics/laptops/gaming`

### 2.4 Query Parameters

Query parameters add some criteria to the request for the resource.

Multiple query parameters can be added by using an `&` ( ampersand ) symbol.

For example,

`http://www.flipkart.com/watches?type=digital&rating=4`

## 3. HTTP

### 3.1 HTTP Requests

HTTP requests are messages sent by the client to initiate an action on the server.

HTTP request includes

- Start Line
- Headers
- Body

#### 3.1.1 Start Line

A Start Line specifies a

- URL
- HTTP Method
- HTTP Version

**HTTP Methods**

The HTTP Request methods indicate the desired action to be performed for a given resource.

| Methods         | Description                                                                                 |
| --------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| GET (Read)      | Request for a resource(s) from the server                                                   |
| POST (Create)   | Submit data to the server                                                                   |
| PUT (Update)    | The data within the request must be stored at the URL supplied, replacing any existing data |
| DELETE (Delete) | Delete a resource(s)                                                                        |

**HTTP Version**

| Year | Version  |
| ---- | -------- |
| 1991 | HTTP/0.9 |
| 1994 | HTTPS    |
| 1996 | HTTP/1.0 |
| 1997 | HTTP/1.1 |
| 2015 | HTTP/2   |
| 2019 | HTTP/3   |

#### 3.1.2 Headers

HTTP Headers let the client and the server to pass **additional information** with an HTTP request or response.

#### 3.1.3 Body

We place the data in the Request body when we want to **send data** to the server.

For example, form details filled by the user.

HTTP Requests

- Start Line
  - URL
    - Protocol
      - HTTP
      - HTTPS
    - Domain Name
    - Path
    - Query Parameters
  - HTTP Method
    - GET (Read)
    - POST (Create)
    - PUT (Update)
    - DELETE (Delete)
  - HTTP Version
- Headers
- Body

### 3.2 HTTP Responses

HTTP responses are **messages** sent by the server as an **answer** to the **clients request**.

HTTP Response includes

- Status Line
- Headers
- Body

#### 3.2.1 Status Line

A Status line specifies a

- HTTP version
- Status code
- Status text

**Status code**

Status codes Indicate whether an HTTP request has been successfully completed or not.

| Status Code Series | Indicates    |
| ------------------ | ------------ |
| 1XX                | Information  |
| 2XX                | Success      |
| 3XX                | Redirection  |
| 4XX                | Client Error |
| 5XX                | Server Error |

- 200 ( Success ) - Indicates that the request has succeeded

- 201 ( Created ) - The request has succeeded and a new resource has been created as a result

**Status text**

| Status Code | Status Text       |
| ----------- | ----------------- |
| 200         | OK                |
| 204         | No Response       |
| 301         | Moved Permanently |
| 401         | Unauthorized      |
| 403         | Forbidden         |
| 404         | Not Found         |

#### 3.2.2 Body

Response Body contains the resource data that was requested by the client.

HTTP Responses

- Status Line
  - HTTP version
  - Status code
    - 1XX
    - 2XX
    - 3XX
    - 4XX
    - 5XX
  - Status text
- Headers
- Body

# Hello Spring Boot
## Concepts Java Frameworks Introduction to Spring Boot Spring and Spring Boot Versions Setting up Spring Boot Project Locally
## 1. Java Frameworks A Java framework is a pre-defined set of libraries and tools that provide a common structure for developing Java-based applications. Frameworks can help developers build applications more quickly and with less code, as they provide a set of standardized components and conventions for common tasks. There are many different Java frameworks available, each with its own set of features and capabilities. Some popular Java frameworks include: **Spring:** Spring is an open-source lightweight framework widely used to develop enterprise (large) applications. Spring Boot is another framework built on top of Spring to build Spring-based applications. **Hibernate:** Hibernate is an object-relational mapping (ORM) framework for Java. It allows developers to map Java objects to database tables and vice versa, making it easier to work with relational data in Java. **JavaServer Faces (JSF):** JSF is a Java-based framework for building web applications. It provides a set of components for building user interfaces and a framework for managing the application's navigation and flow. There are many different Java frameworks available, each with its own set of features and capabilities, so it is important to choose the right one for our specific needs. In this course, we will learn about **Spring Boot**.
## 2. Introduction to Spring Boot Spring Boot is a framework for building Java-based applications. It is built on top of the Spring framework, which is a comprehensive framework for building Java-based applications. - The word **comprehensive framework** here describes that it provides a wide range of features for building Java-based applications. ### 2.1 Why Spring Boot? Spring Boot was introduced to make it easier to create and run Spring-based applications. Before Spring Boot, developers using the Spring framework often had to manually configure a number of components and libraries, which could be time-consuming and error-prone. Additionally, there was no standard way to package and deploy Spring-based applications, which made it difficult to run them in different environments. Spring Boot was introduced to address these issues by providing a number of features that simplify the process of building and deploying Spring-based applications. These features include: - Auto-configuration for various Spring components and libraries - This means that we can get started with a new Spring Boot project quickly, with minimal configuration required. - Support for external configuration, allowing us to easily customize our application's behavior in different environments - A command-line interface (CLI) for quickly creating and running Spring Boot applications While Spring Boot can be used to build a wide range of applications, it is particularly well-suited for building backend applications. It provides a number of features that are useful for building backend services, such as support for data access and transactions, support for building RESTful web services, etc. **Spring Boot is a popular choice if we want to create a web application in Java** Spring Boot is a powerful and convenient framework for building Java-based applications. It can help us build applications more quickly and with less boilerplate code, and it provides a number of useful features that can make our application more robust and easier to maintain.
## 3. Spring Versions The Spring was first released in March 2003. Initially, it had relatively low features and supported less number of technologies. Later on, with every release of newer versions, it supported more technologies and added many features to ease the development process. Spring Framework’s version history
Similar to the JVM, Spring versions are insanely backwards compatible. So, in general, new Spring versions build on top of the older Spring versions and have minimal breaking changes (compared with, say Python 2 vs 3). So, all core concepts for Spring version 3 or 4 are still true for Spring version 5. ## 4. Spring Boot Versions Spring Boot was first released in March 2014. Similar to other softwares, Spring Boot has released many versions by adding new features or extending support to other technologies. Spring Boot's version history
**Spring Boot versions and Java compatibility** - Spring Boot 3.0.0 requires Java 17 as a minimum version. - Spring Boot 2.x supports Java 8 to 19. - If we are using Java 8 or 11, we’ll need to stick to the 2.x release of Spring Boot.
## 5. Setting up Spring Boot Project Locally Let's learn to build a small application using Spring Boot. ### 5.1 Setting up a Spring Boot Project 1. Open [https://start.spring.io](https://start.spring.io/). This service pulls in all the dependencies we need for a Spring Boot application and it does most of the setup for us. 2. Choosing the Project (Gradle or Maven) - Maven and Gradle are build automation tools that are commonly used for Java projects. They allow us to define the dependencies and build steps for our project in a declarative way, using configuration files. - **Maven** is a widely-used build tool for Java projects. It uses configuration files to define the dependencies and build steps for a project. Maven uses a standard directory layout and build lifecycle, which makes it easy to understand and work with. - So, let's select the Maven build tool 3. Selecting the Language - **Java** and **Kotlin** both are object-oriented programming languages and are used for different purposes. - Kotlin is used to develop Android applications while Java is mainly used for developing enterprise (large) applications. - Groovy is a dynamic typing language, while Java is a statically typed language. - Here, select the language as **Java**. 4. Choosing the **Spring Boot Version** - Select Spring Boot 2.x. 5. Additional Project Metadata - Enter the **Group** and **Artifact** names for the project. These are used to identify the project in the generated files and in the Maven build system. - **Group**: In general, the group name is used to identify the organization or company that created the project. It is typically in the form of a reversed domain name, such as _"org.springframework"_, etc. - Let's name our group as `com.example` - **Artifact**: The artifact name is used to identify the specific project within the group. It is a unique name that is assigned to the project, such as _"myproject"_ or _"spring-web"_. - Let's name our project as `helloworld` - Package name: In general, the package names are in a hierarchical naming structure, such as _"com.example.myproject"_ or _"org.springframework.web"_. - In Java, packages with `-` in package name are invalid. So, our package will be `com.example.helloworld`. - Packaging: Let's select the `Jar` - Java: Let's select Java 8, as most companies use Java 8 to build their projects. 6. Adding Dependencies - We will be building backend services using Rest APIs for web applications, so, we need to add **Spring Web** dependency - Spring Data JDBC (can add later on): It gives capabilities to access the database - H2 Database (can add later on): An in-memory database will be created for us to connect data 7. Click on the `Generate` button that generates and downloads the project. To install the Java 8 JDK and maven in our computer, we can use the below command, ``` sudo apt install openjdk-8-jdk maven ``` ### 5.2 Project Structure After generating and downloading the project. It looks as below, - **pom.xml**: It is an XML file that contains information about the project and configuration details used by Maven to build the project - **XML** stands for eXtensible Markup Language. XML is a markup language much like HTML. - **mvnw and mvnw.cmd**: These files are from the Maven wrapper. This allows us to run the Maven project without having Maven installed and present on the path. It downloads the correct Maven version if it's not found. - It means that our project comes with an embedded Maven version and we don't need to download Maven for the whole project to work. **Maven Commands** - **mvn clean**: used to remove the target folder before building the project, which is useful if we want to start with a fresh build. - **mvn install**: used to package the project files into a JAR or WAR file, and install it in the local repository. - **mvn -help**: used to print the maven usage and all the available options for us to use. - **mvn compile**: used to compile the source code of the project. - **mvn test**: used to run the test cases for the project. - **src**: - All the Java classes will be in the package we have created using spring initializer - The package here in our project is `com.example.helloworld` - src -> main -> resources - **application.properties** file: where we can configure our Spring Boot application. - **static** folder: If we want to write HTML pages, static ones or dynamic ones, we can write here. - A main method. - It boots up Spring Boot, which means booting up our embedded web server and after a second we should be able to see something in the browser. ### 5.3 Running Application Run the following command from the terminal to start the application on port **8080**. ``` mvn spring-boot:run ``` A error will be displayed because our Spring Boot application didn’t do anything yet. Now let’s display a **Hello World** text, instead of an error message. ### 5.4 Displaying Hello World Message Let's create a class `HelloWorld` to display **Hello World** text inside the package. - In `HelloWorld` class write a method that returns a **Hello World** text like below, ```java package com.example.helloworld; public class HelloWorld { public String helloWorld() { return "Hello World"; } } ``` In the above code we have written a statement as `package com.example.helloworld;`, in Java, every Java file should have a package statement at the top before any import or class definition. It indicates to which package the class or interface belongs. Spring Boot doesn’t understand what a class is supposed to do. We need to add annotations/decorators to tell Spring Boot to do something with the class. Annotations are similar to the decorators in the Python. They provide additional information about the program to the compiler. Annotations play a key role in Spring Boot and are used to configure and add functionality to the objects that are managed by the Spring Boot framework. - Add `RestController` annotation, ```java package com.example.helloworld; import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController; @RestController public class HelloWorld { public String helloWorld() { return "Hello World"; } } ``` - The `RestController` is from the `org.springframework.web.bind.annotation` package. - The `HelloWorld` class is annotated with the `@RestController` annotation, which indicates that it is a controller class that will handle web requests. - In Spring Boot's approach to building websites, HTTP requests are handled by a controller. - Now, Spring will look all the classes inside our package, when encountered `@RestController` it will create a new instance for the class (HelloWorld). - Map the methods - Spring Boot doesn’t know what to do with `helloWorld()` method. We need to map, it means we should tell the Spring Boot that client (user) will send HTTP GET request to our server and you need to respond to that. - Add `GetMapping` annotation to `helloWorld()` method. The `@GetMapping("/")` annotation is a request mapping annotation in the Spring framework. It is used to map a specific HTTP GET request to a controller method. ```java package com.example.helloworld; import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping; import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController; @RestController public class HelloWorld { @GetMapping("/") public String helloWorld() { return "Hello World"; } } ``` - The `helloWorld()` method will handle HTTP GET requests to the root URL of the application (i.e., path as `/`) and return a **Hello World** text as the response. - The `helloWorld()` method will be executed by spring whenever HTTP GET method is requested with path as `/`. **Spring doesn't automatically reload the application. So, we need to restart the application after every change**
### Summary - A Java framework is a pre-defined set of libraries and tools that provide a common structure for developing Java-based applications. - **Spring** is an open-source lightweight framework widely used to develop enterprise applications. - **Spring Boot** is a comprehensive framework built on top of the Spring framework for building Java-based applications. - **Maven** is a widely-used build tool for Java projects. - The `@RestController` annotation at a class indicates that it is a controller class that will handle HTTP requests. - The `@GetMapping(path)` annotation is a request mapping annotation used to map a specific HTTP GET request to a controller method.

## How to Push your code to GitHub Repository

 <MultiLineNote>
      1. Assuming that you have a GitHub account
      2. Assuming that you have the knowledge to create a new repository otherwise follow this [link](https://learning.ccbp.in/tech-foundations/course?c_id=33a45745-2b2a-4d60-bc16-83ca731081f3&auth_code=yIsdbZUeEbPzrI6go1fIj7hxdC1uu2&s_id=f8f19bee-5d75-4f3b-aa00-5d8b38d23dbe&t_id=339561a7-b259-4dc0-8fdb-ed26bf67263e)
</MultiLineNote>

To push your code to GitHub Repository, Kindly follow the below steps.

#### Step 1: 

- Configuring JAVA IDE to your GitHub Account

- Run this command in the JAVA-IDE terminal to **configure your email ID**

    ```
    git config --global user.email "Enter you email ID here"
    ```

- #### Example:

    ```
    git config --global user.email "rahul@gmail.com"
    ```

-  Run this command in the JAVA-IDE terminal to **configure your name**
    
    ```
    git config --global user.name "Enter your name here"
    ```

    #### Example:
    
    ```
    git config --global user.name "rahul"
    ```

#### Step 2:

- Create an Empty Repository in GitHub

    <SingleLineWarning>
      Don't add the README.md file
    </SingleLineWarning>

- Run this command in the JAVA-IDE terminal to create an empty local Repository

    ```
    git init
    ```

- Run this command in the JAVA-IDE terminal to create a connection between your local repository and remote repository

    ```
            git remote add origin <repositary-url>
    ```

- #### Example:
    
    ```
    git remote add origin https://github.com/phanimurari/Import-and-Export-an-Array.git
    ```

- Run this command to add the code changes in the files to the stage area.

    ```
           git add -A
    ```

- Run this command to save changes to a local repository after staging the changes

    ```
          git commit -m "commit message"
    ```

- #### Example: 

    ```
    git commit -m "solution"
    ```
    
    
    

- Run this command in the JAVA-IDE terminal 

    ```
          git branch -M main
    ```

- Run this command to push your local repository changes to the remote repository

    ```
         git push -u origin main
    ```

- Enter your GitHub Account **username** and **personal access token** to push your code to GitHub Repository.

**Note:** Instead of using a password while authenticating your GitHub account, you have to give your **personal access token**.

You can generate your personal access token by following the below steps.

**`Step 1:`** In the upper-right corner of the page, click your profile photo, then click Settings.

![Image](https://media-content.ccbp.in/ccbp_prod/media/discussion_attachment/a84c5af9-16d0-4825-87f3-f143e14aaf01.jpeg)

**`Step 2:`** In the left sidebar, click `<> Developer settings`.

In the left sidebar, click `<> Developer settings`.

![Image](https://media-content.ccbp.in/ccbp_prod/media/discussion_attachment/a82d7232-cb74-425b-a9e4-7c65c8b83431.jpeg)

**`Step 3:`** In the left sidebar, under **Personal access tokens**, click `Tokens (classic)`.
Select Generate new token In the right sidebar, then click `Generate new token (classic)`.

![Image](https://media-content.ccbp.in/ccbp_prod/media/discussion_attachment/82eaf322-39ff-4300-b6b8-49f495534f56.jpeg)

**`Step 4:`** Enter your GitHub password and then click **Confirm**

![Image](https://media-content.ccbp.in/ccbp_prod/media/discussion_attachment/b25d382e-06cb-454c-aa2a-ade10e3c96de.jpeg)

**`Step 5:`**
- Enter the text in the input element what's this token for
- Select `No expiration` in Expiration section
- Select Repo

![Image](https://media-content.ccbp.in/ccbp_prod/media/discussion_attachment/f596cb8e-761d-43cd-954d-75dde0bec309.jpeg)

Click on Generate token

![Image](https://media-content.ccbp.in/ccbp_prod/media/discussion_attachment/cc6ee0f5-e965-464e-a4ce-fa0bda274c67.jpeg)

**`Step 6:`** You can copy the generated access token

![Image](https://media-content.ccbp.in/ccbp_prod/media/discussion_attachment/c23861f2-fbff-406d-9d15-14a5d21e3c7d.png)

Copy the personal access token and use that personal access token instead of the password to push your code to the remote GitHub repository

<MultiLineNote>
    While pasting the personal access token in the terminal, the personal access token won't be visible in the terminal, so after pasting the personal access token, you can press the `Enter` key.
</MultiLineNote>

Feel free to reach out to us if you are still facing the issue by providing a clear screenshot.

Happy Learning.

# REST APIs
## Concepts REST APIs API Testing Tools: POSTMAN Hands-on with Go REST API GET Authentication & Authorization POST GET by ID PUT DELETE
## Introduction In previous units, we learned about HTTP requests, which are messages sent from a client to a server to request information. The client specifies what action they want to perform (such as getting information or posting new data) using an URL and a method like GET, POST, PUT, or DELETE. The server then sends back an HTTP response, which includes information about the response and a status code indicating the outcome of the request. In this unit, we will explore how to use REST APIs to perform various operations on data, such as creating, reading, updating, and deleting using HTTP requests. ## 1. API API (Application Programming Interface), is a software intermediary that allows two applications to talk to each other. An API defines the rules and format for data exchange between a client and a server. ### REST APIs REST APIs are a type of web APIs that use the Internet to send and receive information. They use common methods such as GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE to interact with data and services on a remote server. REST APIs allow us to create, read, update, and delete data by sending HTTP requests to the server, and receiving HTTP responses with the requested information. The responses from the server are typically returned in a standard format, such as JSON or XML, which makes it easier to use in different programs. ### REST Principles REST(REpresentational State Transfer) is a set of principles that define how Web standards, such as HTTP and URLs, are supposed to be used. Using Rest Principles improves the application in various aspects like scalability, reliability, etc. Some of the Rest Principles are: 1. Providing every resource with a unique ID. For example, - `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/1/` - `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/5/` - `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/10/` - `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/40/` Here, each user has a unique ID which helps to identify and access them. 2. Using standard methods. - GET `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/` - GET `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/:userId/` - POST `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/` - PUT `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/:userId/` - DELETE `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/:userId/` These are the standard methods defined in the HTTP specification with guaranteed behaviour. 3. Accept and Respond with JSON. Here, the client sends a request to the server specifying the data format it wants to receive using the `Content-Type:application/json` header, and the server responds with a JSON content. 4. Statelessness in REST APIs - The server does not store any information about the client's state. Each request is treated independently. - For example, when you access a webpage, the server does not keep track of your previous requests and simply sends back the requested data ### Go REST API Go Rest is an online fake REST API service used for quick testing and prototyping of web and android applications. It provides a simple and convenient way to simulate REST APIs and test their functionality without having to set up a real server or write code. #### Getting Started with Go REST. 1. Open `https://gorest.co.in/` 2. Click on the **login** button in the top right corner. 3. Now click on the **Google** button and Sign in with Google. #### Users API In our practice, we will be using `users` API from Go REST API: - Users API from Go REST API: - Let's look at the data in the users API. #### User Related APIs Go Rest provides different APIs for performing different actions on user data, such as creating, reading, updating, and deleting data.
## 2. API Testing Tools: POSTMAN API testing tools are tools used to test the performance and functionality of APIs. They help make sure APIs work properly and give the right results. There are multiple API testing tools available to test different types of HTTP requests - Postman - Insomnia - SoapUI - Swagger Editor etc. We will be using Postman because it is a popular API testing tool that allows users to send HTTP requests and view the responses. It supports various types of requests (e.g., GET, POST, PUT, DELETE), and provides features for organizing, testing, and documenting APIs. The Postman tool is used by developers to test RESTful APIs and automate API workflows. ### Getting Started with Postman 1. Open the url: `https://www.postman.com/`. 2. Click on **Sign Up for Free**. 3. Create an account by clicking on **Sign Up with Google**. 4. Accept the license agreement. 5. Fill out the basic details and click **Continue without team**. 6. Click on the **Skip for Now** button. 7. Click on the **Let's go** button. 8. Click on **New Http Request** and **Continue**. We completed setting up the Postman. Now we are going to use it to send HTTP requests.
## 3. Hands-on with Go REST API Let's perform some CRUD operations (Create, Read, Update, and Delete) using the Go REST API ### 3.1 GET - Making the HTTP GET request on the users API 1. Copy the users URL `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users` from the Go REST and paste it into the Postman. 2. Select the `GET` method. 3. Click on the send button to send the request. - HTTP Response for the above GET request Here, we got a response from an HTTP GET request. The response includes information about users, a status code **200 OK**, and the format of the response as **JSON**. 1. **200 OK** - 200 is the HTTP status code and OK is the status text. It indicates that the requested resource is available and has been returned to the client in the response message. 2. **JSON** - JSON is a data representation format used for: - Exchanging data between client and server. - Storing data (Client/Server). - JSON is a text-based format that represents data as a collection of key-value pairs and arrays. - JSON supports the following data types. | Data Type | Example | | --------- | ----------------- | | String | "Rahul" | | Number | 9832.32 | | Object | {"name": "rahul"} | | Array | [5, 10, 15] | | Boolean | true | | Null | null | 3. The body tab contains the information of the different users. ### 3.2 Authentication & Authorization #### Authentication Authentication is the process of verifying a user’s identity For example, think of a library card as an example of authentication. In order to enter the library and check out books, we need to prove our identity by presenting a valid library card. #### Authorization Authorization is the process of verifying whether the user is authenticated and determining what a user is allowed to do once they have been authenticated For example, after we've proven our identity by the librarian, our permissions are determined based on our membership level. We may be allowed to check out only books, while a librarian may have access to additional resources such as restricted books, research databases, etc. ### 3.3 POST Let’s make a `POST` request using Postman to create a new user. 1. Click here to open a new tab to make a new HTTP request. 2. Select the POST method. 3. We are adding a user to the user data. So we use users API to add a new user. 4. Select the **Body** tab. 5. Select the **raw** option. 6. The data should be in JSON format, so choose the **JSON** option. 7. Add data in the JSON format and click on the **Send** button. 8. HTTP response for the above POST request. Here, - **401 Unauthorized**: 401 Unauthorized is an HTTP status code indicating that the client is not authorized to access the requested resource and needs to provide a valid access token. - Also received a message **Authentication failed** explaining why the client is not authorized. 9. To get authorization Go REST provides an access token to include in HTTP requests that verifies user identity and allows us to perform a particular action. Now let us see how to get access tokens. 1. Let's go to the home page of Go REST(`https://gorest.co.in/`) and log in. 2. Click on the **API Tokens**. 3. Now let us copy the access token. 10. Now open the **POSTMAN** and select the **Auth** tab. 11. Select the **Bearer Token** option in the `Type` section. 12. Now paste the access token copied from the `Go REST`-->`API TOKEN`. 13. Click on the **Send** button to make the HTTP `POST` request. 14. HTTP response for the above `POST` request. - Here, **201 Created:** **201** is an HTTP status code and **Created** is a status text indicating the successful creation of a new resource on the server as a result of a client's POST request. 15. Upon creating the user, the new ID is added to the user details to identify the user uniquely and is included in the response. Let us see the request we sent and the response we got. - HTTP request We don't need to pass the id in the body because the id is automatically generated by the server to avoid repetitions. - HTTP response Here, the response contains the id as **204476** which is automatically generated. ### 3.4 GET by ID Using the GET method, you can get specific user data based on the ID of the user. 1. We use base url: `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users` + Path: /id to get the data of the specific user. 2. Click on the `+` to open a new tab to create a new HTTP request. 3. Let’s consider the user details that we created in the above POST request. There, the ID is `204476`. So our URL to get the data is `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/204776`. 4. Similar to the POST users API, the GET users API also requires an access token to perform an operation. So click on the **Auth** tab and select the option **Bearer Token**. 5. Now click on the **Send button** to create the HTTP GET request. 6. HTTP response for the above `GET` request. Here, the response contains the user details of id `204476` and the status **200 OK**. ### 3.5 PUT Using the PUT method we can update the specific user data based on the ID of the user. 1. We use base url:`"https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users` + Path: /id to update the data of the specific user. So the URL is `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/204776`. 2. Click on the `+` to open a new tab to create a new HTTP request. 3. Let us update the name of the user we created above from `"Rahul"` to `"Rahul Attuluri"`. 4. Select the method **PUT**. 5. Select **Body**, **raw**, and **JSON** options. 6. Let's update the name in the body section. 7. Similar to the POST users API, the PUT users API also requires an access token to perform an update operation. Select the `Bearer Token` option in the `Auth` tab. 8. Click on the **Send** button to make an HTTP `PUT` request. 9. HTTP response for the above PUT request. Here, the response contains - Status code **200 OK** indicates the user details updated successfully. - The details of the id `204476`. We can see that the name got updated. ### 3.6 DELETE 1. We use base url: `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users` + Path: /id to delete the data of the specific user. So the url is `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/204776`. 2. Click on the `+` to open a new tab to create a new HTTP request. 3. Let us delete the user we created above whose id is `204776`. 4. We use the API `https://gorest.co.in/public/v2/users/204776`. 5. Select the method **DELETE**. 6. Similar to the POST users API, the DELETE users API also requires an access token to perform an operation. So click on the **Auth** tab and select the option **Bearer Token**. 7. Click on the **Send** button to make an HTTP DELETE request. 8. HTTP response for the above DELETE request. Here, **204 No Content:** 204 No Content is an HTTP status code that indicates that the server has successfully processed the request, but there is no content/message to return in the response. This status code is often used in response to a successful `DELETE `request. 9. After deleting a user, if we try to get the deleted user using GET request, we will receive a 404 Not Found response. Let's try to get the deleted user. Here, - **404 Not Found**: 404 Not Found is a HTTP status code that indicates that the server could not find the requested resource. This status code is returned when a client requests a resource that does not exist on the server, or when the server is unable to locate the requested resource. - Also received a message indicating the resource was not found on the server.
### Summary - REST APIs use GET, POST, PUT, and DELETE methods to create, read, update, and delete data on a remote server. - Go Rest API provides resources to perform the CRUD operations. - Postman is an API testing tool that helps us test APIs more easily. - JSON is a data representation format used for exchanging data between client and server. - Authentication and authorization are crucial security mechanisms in REST APIs that determine the identity of a user and control access to resources by enforcing restrictions and permissions.

# Spring Boot with H2 DataBase - Part 1
## Contents Working with Databases H2 Database JDBC Configuring H2 Database Adding Dependencies Providing Configuration Details H2 Web Console Creating Table and Adding Data
## Introduction In the previous unit, we have created a books application that uses APIs to create, read, update, and delete data using the `Book` class and `Bookcontroller` class. We used HashMap to store the data of the books. In this unit, we will learn how to connect to the database in Spring boot. And also learn how to configure the `H2` Database and work with data using the `H2` web console. ## 1. Working with Database Without a database connection, temporary data changes will not be saved. The data changes will be lost every time the server restarts. Spring Boot offers extensive support for working with different databases such as `MySQL`, `SQLite`, `Mongo DB`, `H2`, etc. We will be using `H2` as it is simple to set up and requires minimal setup configurations. ### 1.1 H2 Database `H2` is a Java-based database management system that can be used within a Spring Boot application. It stores data in the computer's disk memory while the application is running, making it faster and easier to use for testing and development. `H2` is commonly used as an alternative to more complex and heavy databases like `MySQL` or `Oracle` during the development and testing phase of an application. When working with `H2`, we can use `SQL` commands to interact with the database, just like with any other relational database management system. So, we use `H2` database in our Spring Boot application. To communicate with the `H2` database and perform various database operations, we use `JDBC`. ### 1.2 JDBC Java Database Connectivity (JDBC) is a standard Java API used to connect Java applications to relational databases. It provides a set of classes and interfaces that allow you to execute SQL statements, retrieve results, and perform other database-related operations. By using JDBC, Java developers can write code that interacts with a wide range of databases without having to worry about the low-level details of each database's API. This makes it much easier and more efficient to develop database-driven applications in Java. Let's configure `H2` database and `JDBC` to use them in our application.
## 2. Configuring H2 Database In Spring Boot, configuring any database is simple and involves only two steps, 1. Adding Dependencies. 2. Providing Configuration Details. ### 2.1 Adding Dependencies #### What is Dependency? In Spring Boot, a dependency is a library that we can use in our application to help us with certain tasks or provide specific features. These libraries are often called "dependencies" because our application depends on them to run correctly. Previously, we used a `Spring Web` dependency that provides a number of libraries and annotations for developing web applications. #### Adding H2 and JDBC Dependencies When we know that these dependencies are needed, we can use the initializer to add dependencies at the time of project creation. The `pom.xml` configuration file contains all the dependencies that are added in the spring initializer. We can add `H2` and `JDBC` dependencies using the initializer.
We can also use the official website & other resources and add a dependency to the pom.xml file to include a specific dependency to the project. **H2 database dependency** ```text com.h2database h2 runtime ``` We can get the above dependency from http://h2database.com/html/build.html. **JDBC dependency** ```text org.springframework.boot spring-boot-starter-data-jdbc ``` - Adding the dependencies to `pom.xml`. ### 2.2 Providing Configuration Details Spring Boot provides a configuration file for setting up various aspects of an application. For example, configure a datasource, security configurations, logging, and version information. - In a Spring Boot Application, the configuration file is usually stored in the `src/main/resources` directory with the name `application.properties`. - We provide the database configuration details in `application.properties` ```text spring.datasource.url = jdbc:h2:file:~/goodreads/src/main/goodreads ``` Here, `spring.datasource.url` is used to specify the URL of the database that the application should connect. Currently, we are connecting to a local database `goodreads` and in the future, we can simply change this URL to connect to a different database. When the application starts, if database `goodreads` does not exist, a file named `goodreads` will be created in the path `~/goodreads/src/main/`. - Let's start the server to see the updated changes in our application.
A file named `goodreads.mv.db` is created in the path `~/goodreads/src/main/`. It uses the `.mv.db` file extension to save its data to disk, which allows you to persist the data even if the application is shut down. Now that we've set up the database, we need to interact with it. One of the major advantages of the `H2` database is its web console, which allows us to interact with `H2` databases through a web browser.
## 3. H2 Web Console The `H2` web console is a web-based interface to interact with an `H2` database using a web browser. It allows us to perform various tasks related to the `H2` database, such as running SQL queries, viewing the schema, reading and updating data. We provide configuration details in the `application.properties` for using the web console. ```text spring.h2.console.enabled=true spring.h2.console.settings.web-allow-others=true ``` Here, - The `spring.h2.console.enabled` property in Spring Boot enables or disables the `H2` web console, a graphical tool for interacting with `H2` database. - The `spring.h2.console.settings.web-allow-others=true`, it means that the H2 console can be accessed from any IP address, not just localhost. Stop the server using CTRL + C and then restart it. Let's go through the `H2` web console. - Copy the Domain server URL. - The default URL path to access the H2 database web console is `/h2-console`.To access the web-console from the browser we have to use the Base URL+ `/h2-console` - The H2 web console login page. - In **JDBC URL**, we have to add the database path used in the `application.properties` file.
- The default `H2` database console user has an empty username and an empty password. - Click on the **Connect** button to log in to the `H2` web console. - `H2` web console home page.
We completed setting up the `H2` web console. We need to create table and add some data to it.
## 4. Creating Table and Adding Data In order to store and manage data in our Spring Boot application, we need to create a database table and add some data to it. ### 4.1 Creating Table There are multiple ways to create tables in an `H2` database 1. Using `H2` console - Using `schema.sql` file etc. #### 4.1.1 Using H2 Console The H2 console allows users to write and run SQL statements
- Let's create a `book` table with columns `ID`, `name`, and `imageURL`. We use the following sql statement to create a `book` table. ```sql create table book ( id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, name varchar(255), imageUrl varchar(255) ); ``` - Click on the run button to create a `book` table.
The SQL statement is executed and creates a `book` table in the database. - Let's write the SQL query to read all the books. ```sql SELECT * FROM BOOK ```
The SQL statement executed and gives an output of empty `book` table with `ID`, `Name`, `IMAGEURL` as columns. Now we delete the existing book table and recreate it by using `schema.sql`. - To delete the existing table we use the following SQL statement. ```sql DROP TABLE BOOK ```
#### 4.1.2 Using `schema.sql` file In a Spring Boot application, the `schema.sql` file is also frequently used to initialize the database schema. It allows us to write SQL statements to create tables. - Create `schema.sql` file in the `~/goodreads/src/main/resources/` path - Adding Configuration details in `application.properties` to use `schema.sql` file in our application. ```text spring.sql.init.mode=always ``` Here, the `spring.sql.init.mode` property is used to control the execution of the `schema.sql` files when the application starts up The value of the this property are as follows: 1. `always`: Execute the SQL statements in `schema.sql` everytime the application starts, regardless of whether the database is empty or not. 2. `embedded`: Execute the SQL statements in `schema.sql` only if the database is empty when using an embedded database. 3. `never`: Do not execute the SQL statements in `schema.sql` at application startup. - Now we write sql statement in the `schema.sql` to create `book` table. ```sql create table if not exists book ( id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT, name varchar(255), imageUrl varchar(255) ); ``` With the `spring.sql.init.mode` set to `always`, the `schema.sql` file is executed each time the application starts up. To prevent the table from being repeatedly created, `if not exists` is used to check if the table already exists before creating it. Instead of using the `if not exists`, we can change the value of `spring.sql.init.mode` to `never` after the application has started. This configuration will prevent the `schema.sql` file from being executed again, even if the application is restarted. We have set up the `schema.sql` file and added its configuration details in `application.properties`. Stop the server using CTRL + C and then restart it. The SQL statement in the `schema.sql` file is executed and creates a `book` table with three columns `ID`. `NAME`, `IMAGEURL`.
We have created an empty `book` table. Now we have to populate data into it. ### 4.2 Adding Data Similar to table creation, we have multiple ways to populate data to the `H2` database 1. Using H2 Console - Using `data.sql` file #### 4.2.1 Using H2 Console We already know that the `H2` console allows users to write and run SQL statements - Let's populate some data using insert statements Use the following SQL statements to insert data into the `book` table: ```sql insert into book(name, imageUrl) values('Harry Potter and the Philosopher''s Stone', 'harry_potter_1.jpg'); insert into book(name, imageUrl) values('Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets','harry_potter_2.jpg'); insert into book(name, imageUrl) values('Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire', 'harry_potter_3.jpg'); insert into book(name, imageUrl) values('Harry Potter and the Cursed Child','harry_potter_4.jpg'); insert into book(name, imageUrl) values('The 3 Mistakes of My Life', 'mistakes_life.jpg'); ``` - Click on the **Run** button to run SQL statements - The SQL queries are executed and 5 books data is populated in the `book` table. - Let's check the data stored in the `book` table.
#### 4.2.2 Using `data.sql` file Similar to the `schema.sql`, the `data.sql` file is also frequently used to populate data to the database tables. It allows us to write SQL statements. We populate the table `book` by creating the `data.sql` file and writing SQL queries in it. - Let's create the `data.sql` file in the `~/goodreads/src/main/resources/`. - Add the SQL statements in `data.sql` to insert the data into `book` table. Use the following queries to insert data: ```sql insert into book(name, imageUrl) values('Life of Pi', 'life_of_pi.jpg'); insert into book(name, imageUrl) values('One Night ...','one_night_acc.jpg'); insert into book(name, imageUrl) values('Half Girlfriend', 'half_gf.jpg'); insert into book(name, imageUrl) values('The Secret', 'secret.jpg'); insert into book(name, imageUrl) values('Rise', 'rise.jpg'); ``` - We need to provide configuration details of the `data.sql` in `application.properties` to use it in our application. ```text spring.sql.init.mode=always ``` The same `spring.sql.init.mode=always` property is used to control the execution of the `data.sql` files when the application starts up. We used the `if not exists` clause in the `schema.sql` file to prevent the table from being created again if it already exists. This ensures that when the application runs, only the statements in `data.sql` file will be executed. Stop the server using `CTRL + C` and then restart it. - Let's check the data stored in the `book` table.
We completed creating the table and adding data to it. Let's change the value of `spring.sql.init.mode` in `application.properties` to `never`.
Here, we updated the `spring.sql.init.mode` value to `never` to avoid the execution of the `data.sql` and `schema.sql` files, as we already have the `book` table and the data of books in it. In the next unit, we will write REST APIs using the `H2` database to store and retrieve data in our `Goodreads` application.
### Summary - Working with H2 databaese - Configuring H2 Database - Adding Dependencies - H2 Database - Spring Data JDBC - Providing Configuration Details - application.properties - H2 Database - Interacting with H2 database using H2 web console - Creating Tables - Using H2 Console - Using schema.sql - Populating Data - Using H2 Console - Using data.sql

<Section id="1-introduction">

## Introduction:
Spring Framework is a powerful and widely used open-source application development framework for building enterprise-grade Java applications. It provides a comprehensive infrastructure that simplifies the development of complex applications by offering a range of features and tools that enable developers to create scalable, maintainable, and robust applications.

One of the key features of Spring is its modular architecture, which allows developers to choose which components they need for their specific projects. This modular approach makes it easy to manage dependencies, enhance code reusability, and improve maintainability.
</Section>

<Section id="2-core-components-of-spring-framework">

## 1. Core Components of Spring Framework:
Spring Framework has a vast ecosystem of concepts, including

    i. Dependency Injection
    ii. Inversion of Control
    iii. Aspect Oriented Programming(AOP)
    iv. Spring Batch Processing
    v. Spring Integration
    vi. Spring cloud

- At its core, Spring framework is really just a dependency injection container, with a couple of convenience layers (think: database access, proxies, aspect-oriented programming, RPC, a web mvc framework) added on top. It helps you build Java application faster and more conveniently.
- In this reading document, we will be mainly focussing on Dependency Injection, Inversion of Control, and it's implementation. Remaining topics will be covered in the upcoming sessions.
  </Section>

<Section id="3-dependency-injection">

## 2. Dependency Injection:
Dependency injection is a design pattern that is commonly used in software development, particularly in object-oriented programming. The basic idea behind dependency injection is that objects should be given their dependencies rather than creating them internally.

In simpler terms, dependency injection is a way to pass objects (dependencies) to a class instead of the class creating them itself. This makes the class more modular, flexible, and testable.

Let's say we have two classes, `Car` and `Engine`. The `Car` class depends on the `Engine` class to run. Traditionally, we would create the `Engine` object inside the `Car` class like this:

```java
public class Car {
        private Engine engine;
        public Car() {
            this.engine = new Engine();
        }
}
```
However, this approach is inflexible and can make it difficult to test the `Car` class in isolation. Instead, we can use dependency injection to pass the `Engine` object to the `Car` class from outside:

```java
public class Car {
    private Engine engine;

    public Car(Engine engine) {
        this.engine = engine;
    }
}
```
In this case, the Car class no longer creates the Engine object itself. Instead, the Engine object is created outside the Car class and passed to it as a parameter when the Car object is created. This is known as constructor injection.

Now, let's create an instance of the Engine class and pass it to the Car class:

```java
public static void main(String[] args) {
    Engine engine = new Engine();
    Car car = new Car(engine);
}
```
By using dependency injection, we have decoupled the `Car` and `Engine` classes, making them more modular and easier to test. We can now easily substitute the `Engine` object with a mock object for testing purposes or create different types of `engines` for different types of `cars`.
</Section>

<Section id=3-inversion-of-control">

## 3. Inversion of Control
In software engineering, Inversion of Control (IoC) is a design pattern that allows the control of object creation, flow of control, and object lifecycle management to be shifted from the application code to an external framework or container. This pattern is also known as the Dependency Injection (DI) pattern.

In traditional programming, a program creates objects and controls the flow of execution by calling methods on those objects. In contrast, in IoC, the flow of control is inverted, and the framework manages the creation and execution of objects.

The IoC pattern consists of two components:

#### I. Container
The container is responsible for the following tasks:

- Creating objects: The container creates and initializes the objects that are required by the application.

- Configuring objects: The container configures the objects by setting their properties and injecting their dependencies.

- Managing object lifecycle: The container manages the lifecycle of the objects, including creating, destroying, and reusing them.

- Wiring objects together: The container wires the objects together by injecting the dependencies of one object into another object.

#### II. Components
The components are the objects that provide the functionality of the application.
- The components are responsible for the following tasks:

- Providing functionality: The components provide the functionality of the application.

- Declaring dependencies: The components declare their dependencies on other components and services.

- Implementing interfaces: The components implement interfaces that define their behavior.

The IoC pattern provides several benefits, including:

- Decoupling of components: The IoC pattern decouples the components of an application, making it easier to replace or modify them without affecting other components.

- Testability: The IoC pattern makes it easier to write unit tests for individual components because their dependencies can be easily mocked or stubbed.

- Re-Usability: The IoC pattern promotes the reuse of components by making them more modular and easier to integrate into other applications.

- Scalability: The IoC pattern makes it easier to scale an application by allowing the container to manage the creation and lifecycle of objects.

In conclusion, Inversion of Control is a design pattern that allows the control of object creation, flow of control, and object lifecycle management to be shifted from the application code to an external framework or container. This pattern provides several benefits, including decoupling of components, testability, reusability, and scalability.
</Section>
<Section id ="4-implementation-of-ioc-using-dependency-injection" >

## 4. Implementation of IoC using Dependency Injection:
In Spring Framework for Java, IoC is implemented using Dependency Injection (DI) through the use of the Spring IoC container. Here's an example implementation of IoC using DI in Spring Framework for Java:

Here’s JdbcTemplate implementation using Constructor injection:
In one of the previous sessions of JdbcTemplate, we implemented it using constructor injection.

```java
@Service
public class BookH2Service implements BookRepository {
    private JdbcTemplate db;

    public DataSource dataSource() {
        HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig();
        config.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:h2:file:~/Workspace/content/java-spring-code-samples/spring-boot/src/main/resources/booksdb");
        return new HikariDataSource(config);
    }

    public BookH2Service(JdbcTemplate db) {
        db.setDataSource(dataSource());
        this.db = db;
    }
}
```

And the constructor argument is called from BookController in the following way:

```java
@RestController
public class BookController {
    private final BookH2Service bookH2Service;

    public BookController() {
        this.bookH2Service = new BookH2Service(new JdbcTemplate());
    }
}
```
Next, we'll modify the BookH2Service class to use Dependency Injection. In this modified version, the BookH2Service class takes JdbcTemplate instances as constructor arguments, instead of creating them itself.

Instead of a module or class controlling the flow of execution, the control is transferred to an external source, usually an IoC container, which manages the objects and their dependencies.

Let's look at the new modified BookH2Service.

```java
@Service
public class BookH2Service implements BookRepository {
    private JdbcTemplate db;
    public BookH2Service(JdbcTemplate db){
        this.db = db;
    }
}
```
Identify the dependencies that the component requires to function correctly.

This is an example of Dependency Injection, because we're injecting the dependencies (i.e. JdbcTemplate ) into the BookH2Service class from an external source.
Now, we'll create a bean class that creates instance of JdbcTemplate using Inversion of Control:

Define the Spring configuration class: Define a Spring configuration class that specifies the beans and their dependencies using the `@Configuration` and `@Bean` annotations.

```java
@Configuration
public class AppConfig {
    @Bean
    public DataSource dataSource() {
        HikariConfig config = new HikariConfig();
        config.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:h2:file:~/Workspace/content/java-spring-code-samples/spring-boot/src/main/resources/booksdb");
        return new HikariDataSource(config);
    }

    @Bean
    public JdbcTemplate jdbcTemplate() {
        return new JdbcTemplate(dataSource());
    }
}
```
In the above code, `@Configuration` annotation indicates that this `AppConfig` class contains Spring configuration metadata. This metadata is used by the spring container to create and manage beans.

`@Bean`: here a bean is a Spring-managed objects that can be used throughout the application. This spring-managed objects are created, injected and managed through their whole life time in an application. @Bean is an annotation used to indicate that a method in a spring configuration class should be used to create and configure a bean.

When Spring starts up, it reads the configuration classes and creates beans based on the bean definitions in those classes. Each bean is created and initialized before it is injected into any dependent objects.

Once all the beans have been created and initialized, Spring creates instances of the dependent objects and injects the beans into them. This includes constructor injection, where Spring resolves the constructor arguments and injects the appropriate beans.

A class annotated with `@Configuration` can contain methods annotated with `@Bean`, which create and configure the beans that the Spring container manages. The method body contains the logic to create and configure the bean.
</Section>

<Section id = 5-summary>

## 5. Summary
Overall, the @Configuration annotation is an important part of Spring's configuration model, and is used to create and manage beans that make up a Spring application.

In this example, we use the **`@Bean`** annotation to create instances of `JdbcTemplate` and `DataSource.` We're using Inversion of Control here because we're allowing the Spring container to manage the creation and injection of these objects, instead of creating them ourselves in the `BookH2Service`class.

Here when from `BookH2Service` class, JdbcTemplate is called, it checks for bean classes in `AppConfig` class and implements that particular bean class. In this bean class, it has bean method call of `dataSource()` which is implemented as another bean class which in turn can be used by multiple other bean methods but here we are only using it inside one bean method. Thus it create an instance of JdbcTemplate with the required dataSource and injects this dependency instance into the `BookH2Service` class without altering the main or principle code.
</Section>
